q: PTA-driven Continuous Accounts Discovery can automatically onboard an unmanaged privileged account it sees being used. Which target types does it support out of the box?
opts: Windows only
Windows, UNIX, AWS and Azure — anything else needs a custom PTA plug-in
Any platform that exists in the Vault
Only cloud platforms
why: Continuous discovery is PTA noticing a connection made with a privileged account that is not stored in the Vault, and reacting. Out of the box that detection-and-onboard path covers Windows, UNIX, AWS and Azure; extending it to anything else means writing a custom PTA plug-in. PTA also continuously monitors Windows local Administrators groups for newly privileged accounts.
wrong: A is too narrow, C too broad, D omits the two on-premises platforms that make up most of the value.

q: When an onboarding rule is created through the REST API, which filter is mandatory?
opts: `UserNameFilter`
`SystemTypeFilter` — Windows or Unix
`AddressFilter`
`IsAdminIDFilter`
why: `SystemTypeFilter` is the one mandatory filter, alongside the mandatory targets `TargetPlatformId` and `TargetSafeName`. Everything else — username, address, machine type, account category — is optional narrowing.
wrong: A, C and D are all real optional filters. `UserNameFilter` is capped at 512 characters and pairs with `UserNameMethod`; `AddressFilter` pairs with `AddressMethod`; `IsAdminIDFilter` is a boolean.

q: An onboarding rule's `UserNameMethod` and `AddressMethod` accept which values?
opts: Equals, Begins, Ends
Contains, Regex, Exact
Include, Exclude
StartsWith, EndsWith, Wildcard
why: Both matching methods take Equals, Begins or Ends. That is deliberately simple — rules are meant to be predictable and auditable, so there is no regular-expression matching here.
wrong: B, C and D all offer richer matching than the rule engine actually supports. Note the contrast with `AllowedSafes` on a platform, which *is* a regular expression — do not mix the two up.

q: Which values can an onboarding rule's Machine type and Account category filters take?
opts: Machine type: Any / Workstation / Server. Account category: Any / Privileged / Non-privileged
Machine type: Windows / Unix. Account category: Local / Domain
Machine type: Physical / Virtual. Account category: Service / Interactive
Machine type: Server / Endpoint. Account category: Tier 0 / Tier 1 / Tier 2
why: `MachineTypeFilter` is Any, Workstation or Server; `AccountCategoryFilter` is Any, Privileged or Non-privileged. Together with system type and a keyword these are what let you route, say, privileged accounts on servers into one Safe and workstation accounts into another.
wrong: B confuses machine type with system type. C and D invent categories that do not exist in the rule dialog.

q: You want a Windows discovery to run every week rather than once. Where is that set?
opts: It cannot be — discovery is always a one-off and must be re-run manually
In the Accounts Discovery definition itself, which supports a one-time scan or a recurring schedule
With a Windows scheduled task on the CPM server calling the scanner binary
In the Master Policy
why: Recurrence is part of the discovery definition in the PVWA. Making the scan recurring is what turns discovery from a one-off inventory exercise into an ongoing control, so newly created privileged accounts keep surfacing in Pending Accounts.
wrong: A and C describe workarounds for a capability that is built in. D is unrelated — the Master Policy governs access workflows, not discovery.

q: Which permission does a user need to obtain a copy of an SSH private key stored in the Vault?
opts: Use Accounts
List Accounts
Retrieve Accounts
Initiate CPM account management operations
why: An SSH private key is retrieved exactly like a password: List Accounts to see it, Retrieve Accounts to get a copy of the secret itself. This is why the same split-workflow logic applies — a user who only needs to connect gets Use, not Retrieve.
wrong: A gives Connect through the PSM, not the key material. B only reveals that the account exists. D exposes the Change / Verify / Reconcile buttons.
ref: Safe member permissions / SSH key management

q: Besides Windows Services, Scheduled Tasks and IIS Application Pools, which two dependency types can Windows discovery detect? (Choose two)
opts: IIS Anonymous Access
COM+ Applications
Registry keys holding credentials
ODBC connection strings
why: The discoverable set is Windows services, scheduled tasks, IIS application pools, IIS anonymous access and COM+ applications — all of them registered in a machine's own configuration surface, so they can be enumerated programmatically.
wrong: C and D are credentials embedded in arbitrary storage. The CPM can manage them once you add them by hand, but nothing can reliably find them by scanning.

q: Which onboarding sources use the "Add discovered accounts" REST method? (Choose three)
opts: The CPM Scanner
PTA
DNA (Discovery & Audit)
PARestore
why: "Add discovered accounts" is the ingestion path for anything that *discovers* — the CPM Scanner, PTA's continuous discovery, DNA and third-party scanners. Crucially, accounts arriving this way are evaluated against the automatic onboarding rules; accounts added with the plain "Add account" method are not.
wrong: D is a backup restore utility, not a discovery source.

q: Which statement about manually adding an account in the PVWA is correct?
opts: The address, username, platform and Safe are all required; the platform then determines which additional properties are mandatory
Only the username and password are required
The Safe is optional and defaults to PasswordManagerShared
The platform is chosen automatically from the address
why: Every account needs a location on the network (address), an identity (username), a Safe to live in and a target account platform to be governed by. The platform then dictates the rest — some platforms add mandatory properties such as a port, database name or domain.
wrong: B omits the two structural requirements. C and D are wrong: neither Safe nor platform is ever inferred, because both are deliberate access-control and policy decisions.

q: PTA has detected an unmanaged AWS IAM access key in use. Which automatic remediation actions can PTA take? (Choose three)
opts: Onboard the unmanaged account into the Vault
Rotate the credential
Reconcile the credential
Delete the IAM user
why: PTA's automatic containment set is onboard, rotate and reconcile — bringing the credential under management and invalidating whatever the attacker may hold. For AWS specifically it detects unmanaged access keys and passwords for IAM accounts, compromised privileged IAM accounts and compromised EC2 accounts.
wrong: D is destructive and outside PTA's remit — containment is about taking control of the credential, not deleting the identity. Where PSM is integrated, PTA can also suspend or terminate a live session.

q: Which onboarding path evaluates accounts against the automatic onboarding rules?
opts: "Add account" in the PVWA
"Add multiple accounts from a file" (bulk CSV upload)
"Add discovered accounts" — the path used by the CPM Scanner, PTA and DNA
Restoring a Safe with PARestore
why: Onboarding rules exist to triage *discovered* accounts. Only accounts arriving through the discovery ingestion path are compared against them; if none matches, the account lands in Pending Accounts for a human to place.
wrong: A and B are both deliberate acts where the operator has already chosen the Safe and platform, so there is nothing for a rule to decide. D is a restore operation.

q: What must the first row of a bulk-upload CSV contain?
opts: The Safe name that all accounts will go into
A header row of account property names
A count of the accounts in the file
The platform ID
why: The first row is a header naming the properties each column carries, so the upload can map columns to account properties — including platform-specific ones. Downloading the sample CSV from the Add accounts from file window is the reliable way to get the header right.
wrong: A and D are per-account column values, not file-level headers — different rows can target different Safes and platforms. C is not part of the format.
ref: Add multiple accounts from a file

q: Before an onboarding rule that references a reconcile account can run successfully, what must be true?
opts: The reconcile account must already exist, per the rule's definition, alongside the target Safe
The CPM will create the reconcile account on first use
Reconcile accounts cannot be referenced by onboarding rules
The reconcile account must be in the Pending Accounts list
why: The documented prerequisite is to create the Safe *and* the reconcile account according to the rule's definition before the rule runs. A rule places accounts into a prepared structure; it does not build the structure.
wrong: B — nothing is auto-created. C is false. D confuses a working reconcile account with a discovered one.

q: Which of these best describes how CyberArk now recommends sequencing an onboarding programme?
opts: Onboard the largest account populations first to show rapid coverage numbers
Work through a risk-versus-effort prioritisation — highest risk reduction for lowest implementation effort first
Follow the five Blueprint stages in strict order
Onboard alphabetically by Safe name so nothing is missed
why: The Blueprint's five-stage model was retired in August 2024 and replaced by a risk-effort index: a prioritisation matrix weighing the risk impact of a use case against the effort to implement it. In practice that still puts Tier 0 first, but the framing is now explicitly about return on effort rather than a fixed sequence.
wrong: A optimises for a metric that does not reduce risk. C is the retired model — still taught in v12.6 material, so know it exists, but know it has been superseded. D is arbitrary.

q: Which statement about discovered SSH keys is correct?
opts: They are discovered by Windows discovery
UNIX discovery returns them along with local accounts, including the trust relationships between machines
They can only be added manually
They are stored outside the Vault, on the CPM
why: UNIX discovery enumerates local accounts and SSH keys, and mapping the authorized/trusted key relationships is often the more valuable output — key-based trust paths are exactly how an attacker moves laterally across a UNIX estate.
wrong: A — Windows discovery has no SSH keys to find. C is false. D is false: keys are vaulted objects, protected like any other secret. Note that once a key is imported it should be rotated immediately, because the act of entering it exposed it.
ref: Accounts Discovery — UNIX / onboard SSH keys

q: Which ports does PTA use to communicate with the Vault and the DR Vault?
opts: TCP 443 only
TCP and UDP 1858
TCP 9022
UDP 514
why: PTA needs both TCP and UDP on 1858 to the Vault and to the DR Vault — it consumes the Vault's activity stream as well as making requests. Administrator access to the PTA itself is over TCP 80/443.
wrong: A is the PVWA's user-facing port. C is the Remote Control Client to PARAgent. D is syslog, which is how PTA *receives* logs from other sources, not how it talks to the Vault.

q: PVWA-to-PTA calls have started failing. Which account is involved, and what is the documented remedy?
opts: `PVWAGWUser` — recreate its credential file
`PTA_PAS_Gateway` — re-sync the PTA Vault users by running `VaultPermissionsValidation.sh` in the PTA server's utility folder
`PasswordManager` — reset its password in the PrivateArk Client
`Backup` — enable the user and set a password
why: `PTA_PAS_Gateway` is the account used for REST calls between the PVWA and PTA. When that link breaks, the fix is to re-synchronise the PTA Vault users and that account by running `VaultPermissionsValidation.sh` from the utility folder on the PTA server — reachable with the `UTILITYDIR` alias.
wrong: A is the PVWA's gateway impersonation user. C is the CPM's user. D is the backup user used by PAReplicate.

q: From version 14.0 onwards, where are PTA settings configured?
opts: Only on the PTA appliance's own console
In the PVWA interface
In `dbparm.ini` on the Vault
In the PrivateArk Client
why: Version 14.0 moved PTA settings into the PVWA, alongside CIS Level 2 hardening on RHEL 8, event closure reasons and richer email notifications carrying Event and Session IDs. It is a good example of the general direction: configuration consolidating into the web interface.
wrong: A was the older model. C configures the Vault, not PTA. D manages Vault users, groups and Safes.

q: What is the purpose of listing more than one address in a component's `Vault.ini`?
opts: Load balancing across multiple production Vaults
Failover — the component tries the next address if the first is unreachable, which is how components find the DR Vault after a failover
Replication configuration
Specifying the PVWA and the Vault together
why: `Vault.ini` holds the Vault's address and port, and multiple addresses can be listed comma-separated. On failover the component works down the list, which is what lets CPMs, PVWAs and PSMs reattach to the DR Vault without being reconfigured by hand.
wrong: A — the Vault is not load balanced this way. C is `PADR.ini`. D — the PVWA is not referenced in Vault.ini.

q: A task requires setting a Vault-level authorization and creating a Network Area. Which interface do you use?
opts: The PVWA
The PrivateArk Client
PACLI
The Remote Control Client
why: The PrivateArk Client is the administrative interface for Vault-level objects: users and their Vault authorizations, groups, Network Areas, Safe properties such as the Restrictions tab, and Safe renaming. The PVWA is the day-to-day interface for accounts, Safes membership, platforms and policy.
wrong: A does not expose Network Areas. C is a scripting interface to Vault data. D controls Vault services remotely over 9022.

q: Which component sends email notifications from the Vault, and which Safe supports it?
opts: The PVWA, using `PVWAConfig`
The ENE (Event Notification Engine), using the `Notification Engine` Safe
The CPM, using `PasswordManagerShared`
PTA, using `VaultInternal`
why: The Notification Engine is one of the three Safes created at Vault installation — `Notification Engine`, `System` and `VaultInternal` — and the ENE service uses it to hold notification configuration and templates. It relays over SMTP on port 25, and writes `ENEConsole.log` and `ENETrace.log`.
wrong: A, C and D each name a real Safe belonging to a different component. `PVWAConfig` holds `PVConfiguration.xml` and `Policies.xml`; `PasswordManagerShared` holds platform definitions.

q: Which file holds the Vault's SNMP settings, and which parameters would you set there?
opts: `dbparm.ini` — `Syslog`, `SyslogServerIP`
`paragent.ini` — `SNMPHostIP`, `SNMPTrapPort`, `SNMPCommunity`
`tsparm.ini` — `SNMPTarget`
`my.ini` — `Server-id`
why: `paragent.ini` configures the Remote Control Agent, and SNMP trap delivery is part of that agent's job — hence `SNMPHostIP`, `SNMPTrapPort` and `SNMPCommunity` living there rather than in the main Vault configuration.
wrong: A is where syslog/SIEM forwarding is configured — a different monitoring channel. C defines where the Safes are located on disk. D is database configuration.

q: Which statement about forwarding Vault audit data to a SIEM is correct?
opts: It is configured in `dbparm.ini` and sent over syslog, typically on port 514
It requires EVD to run on a schedule
It is configured in the PVWA under Reports
It uses the Remote Control Agent on 9022
why: Syslog forwarding is a Vault-level setting in `dbparm.ini`, streaming audit records continuously to the SIEM over port 514 (TLS, TCP or UDP). Like every `dbparm.ini` change it needs a Vault restart to take effect.
wrong: B describes EVD, which is a pull-based export for custom reporting rather than a continuous feed. C generates reports into `PVWAReports`. D is service control.

q: Why does CyberArk care about NTP configuration across PAM components?
opts: It is only cosmetic — log timestamps look neater
Clock skew breaks Kerberos authentication, certificate validation and the correlation of audit records across components
NTP is required for the Vault licence to validate
It controls the CPM processing interval
why: Time is load-bearing in a PAM deployment. Kerberos rejects tickets outside a tight clock skew window, certificate validity checks depend on accurate time, and any forensic reconstruction depends on Vault, CPM, PSM and target logs agreeing on when things happened. Windows components are typically pointed at a reliable source with `w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:… /syncfromflags:manual /reliable:YES /update`.
wrong: A trivialises a real dependency. C and D are invented.

q: What is the maximum size of a Distributed Vault deployment?
opts: Two servers — one primary and one DR
Six servers — one Primary and five Satellites
Ten servers in an active-active cluster
Unlimited, limited only by licence
why: A Distributed Vault tops out at six servers: one Primary plus five Satellites. Satellites serve read requests locally to reduce latency for geographically dispersed sites, while writes go to the Primary.
wrong: A describes a classic Vault plus DR pair. C confuses it with Cluster Vault, which is a two-node active-passive arrangement for local high availability. D is wrong — the limit is architectural.
